summary: To kill: the plain word for taking life, used of Cain killing Abel, of murder and of the slaughter of war, of the killing the law commanded, of beasts, and of Yahweh slaying in judgment. It is not limited to murder, which is רָצַח: the same verb names lawful execution (Lev 20:15; Deu 13:10) and Yahweh's own acts (Exo 4:23; Psa 78:34), and “a time to kill” stands against “a time to heal” (Ecc 3:3). The nouns הֶרֶג and הֲרֵגָה are slaughter, above all in “the valley of slaughter”, the new name of the valley of Hinnom (Jer 7:32), and “the flock of slaughter” (Zec 11:4). Moabite, Sabaic, Ugaritic and Aramaic have the same verb “kill”, and Arabic harj is slaughter.

words.gloss: kill, slay; put to death; destroy
words.summary: About 165 times, nearly all qal. Its subject may be a man, an army, the people carrying out the law, a beast, or Yahweh; its object is almost always living, a man or beast, and only by extension vines, or the fool whom vexation kills. Its passive participle הֲרוּגִים is “the slain”. Beside הֵמִית “put to death” it is the more general word (Deu 13:10; 2Sa 3:30; Job 5:2).

stems.gloss: kill, slay; put to death; destroy; (passive participle) the slain

senses.definition: To take a man's life by violence, openly or by guile: Cain's killing of Abel, the killing feared by Cain, Jacob and Moses, the killing of Abner, the prophets and Zechariah son of Jehoiada.

evidence.note: “Cain rose up against Abel his brother וַיַּהַרְגֵהוּ”: the first killing.
“Whoever finds me will kill me (יַהַרְגֵנִי).”
Seth given “instead of Abel, for Cain killed him”.
Esau: “then I will kill Jacob my brother.”
“Come, let us kill him and throw him into one of the pits.”
“Do you mean to kill me (הַלְהָרְגֵנִי) as you killed (הָרַגְתָּ) the Egyptian?”: Moses had struck him dead (Exo 2:12). Quoted in Act 7:28.
“If a man acts presumptuously against his neighbour to kill him (לְהָרְגוֹ) with guile, you shall take him from my altar to die.”
“Joab and Abishai his brother killed (הָרְגוּ) Abner, because he had put to death (הֵמִית) Asahel their brother”: the two verbs of one deed.
“They have killed your prophets with the sword”; quoted in Rom 11:3.
Joash “killed his son”, Zechariah son of Jehoiada, who said as he died, “May Yahweh see and require it.” Compare Mat 23:35.
The adversaries: “we will come into their midst and kill them, and stop the work.”
“Do you want to kill (ἀνελεῖν) me as you killed the Egyptian yesterday?”: Exo 2:14.

senses.definition: To slay in numbers, in battle or after it: the kings and men of Midian, the men of Ai, the seventy sons of Gideon, the enemies of the Jews.

evidence.note: “They warred against Midian … and killed every male; and the kings of Midian they killed with the rest of their slain.”
When Israel had finished killing all the inhabitants of Ai in the field.
Abimelech “killed his brothers the sons of Jerubbaal, seventy men, on one stone”.
David slew of Aram seven hundred chariots and forty thousand horsemen.
“In Shushan the citadel the Jews killed and destroyed five hundred men.”
They “killed of those who hated them seventy-five thousand”.
“You have slain (הָרַגְתָּ) in the day of your anger; you have slaughtered (טָבַחְתָּ) without pity.”

senses.definition: Of Yahweh: to put to death in judgment, by the plagues of Egypt, the sword, hail, the word of his prophets, or the beasts he sends.

evidence.note: “Behold, I will kill your son, your firstborn.”
“Yahweh killed every firstborn in the land of Egypt.”
“My anger will burn, and I will kill you with the sword” (of those who afflict the widow and fatherless).
“The anger of God rose against them and killed of their fattest.”
“When he slew them (הֲרָגָם), then they sought him, and returned and sought God earnestly.”
“Who struck many nations and slew mighty kings.”
“I slew your young men with the sword … yet you did not return to me.”
“From there I will command the sword, and it will slay them.”
“I have hewn them by the prophets; I have slain them by the words of my mouth.”
In that day Yahweh “will slay the dragon that is in the sea”.
“Yahweh sent lions among them, and they were killing (הֹרְגִים) among them.”

senses.definition: To kill at Yahweh's command: the beast in a capital crime, the one who entices to other gods, the men who joined themselves to Baal-peor.

evidence.note: The man “shall surely be put to death (מוֹת יוּמָת), and the beast you shall kill (תַּהֲרֹגוּ)”.
“You shall surely kill him (הָרֹג תַּהַרְגֶנּוּ); your hand shall be first upon him to put him to death (לַהֲמִיתוֹ).”
“Each kill his brother, his companion and his neighbour”: the Levites at the calf.
“Kill each of you his men who joined themselves to Baal-peor.”
“A time to kill (לַהֲרוֹג) and a time to heal”: killing in its season, the opposite of healing.

senses.definition: To kill a beast, or of a beast to kill.

evidence.note: Balaam to his ass: “If there were a sword in my hand, I would kill you now.”
“Slaying oxen (הָרֹג בָּקָר) and killing sheep, eating flesh and drinking wine.”
“The tongue of the viper will slay him.”

senses.definition: Of things that are not killed by a blow: vines struck by hail, the fool brought down by his own vexation, the simple by their turning away.

evidence.note: “He killed (יַהֲרֹג) their vines with hail, and their sycamores with frost.”
“Vexation kills (יַהֲרָג) the fool, and jealousy puts to death (תָּמִית) the simple.”
“The turning away of the simple will kill them.”
“I will kill your root with famine, and it will slay your remnant.”

senses.definition: The passive participle הֲרוּגִים: those who have been killed, lying dead.

evidence.note: “Come from the four winds, O breath, and breathe into these slain (בַּהֲרוּגִים), that they may live.”
“The earth will disclose her blood, and will no more cover her slain (הֲרוּגֶיהָ).”
“Many are the fallen (חֲלָלִים) she has cast down, and mighty are all her slain (הֲרֻגֶיהָ).”

senses.definition: The passive of the qal: to be slain, by the sword or in a slaughter.

evidence.note: “Shall priest and prophet be slain (יֵהָרֵג) in the sanctuary of the Lord?”
“Her daughters in the field will be slain by the sword.”
“When the wounded groan, when slaughter is wrought (בֵּהָרֵג הֶרֶג) in your midst.”

senses.definition: To be killed. Both forms may be a qal passive.

evidence.note: “Or is he slain (הֹרָג) as the slaying (כְּהֶרֶג) of his slain (הֲרֻגָיו)?”
“For your sake we are killed (הֹרַגְנוּ) all the day; we are counted as sheep for slaughter (טִבְחָה).”
Paul quotes Psa 44:22 (Hebrew 44:23) of those in Christ: “for your sake we are being put to death (θανατούμεθα) all the day long”, yet nothing separates them from the love of God (Rom 8:37–39).
“Lord, they have killed (ἀπέκτειναν) your prophets”: Elijah's words of 1Ki 19:10, 14.

evidence.locator: Exo.2.14, הַלְהָרְגֵנִי → ἀνελεῖν, הָרַגְתָּ → ἀνεῖλες; ἀναιρέω renders הָרַג ×14

evidence.note: Stephen quotes Exo 2:14: “Do you want to kill me as you killed the Egyptian yesterday?”

evidence.locator: Psa.44.23, הֹרַגְנוּ → θανατούμεθα; θανατόω renders הָרַג ×4

evidence.note: Psa 44:23 quoted: “for your sake we are being put to death all the day long.”

parallels.note: Hiphil of מוּת, “put to death”: set beside הָרַג of the same act.
“Slaughter”, as of beasts: the killing of men likened to the butcher's.
“Pierced, fallen”: the dead of battle beside “the slain”.

evidence.note: “The ones killing you (הֹרְגֶךָ) … the ones piercing you (מְחַלְלֶיךָ).”

opposites.note: “Heal”: a time to kill and a time to heal.
“Live”: the slain made to live by the breath.

senses.definition: A killing, especially of many: slaughter in war or judgment.

evidence.note: “The Jews struck all their enemies with the stroke of the sword, and slaughter (וְהֶרֶג), and destruction.”
“Deliver those taken to death (לַמָּוֶת), and those staggering to slaughter (לַהֶרֶג).”
Streams of water on every high hill “in the day of great slaughter, when the towers fall”.
“When slaughter is wrought (בֵּהָרֵג הֶרֶג) in your midst.”
“As the slaying (כְּהֶרֶג) of his slain.”

parallels.note: “Death”: those taken to death, staggering to slaughter.

senses.definition: Slaughter, in Jeremiah and Zechariah always of a coming judgment: the valley, the day and the flock marked for it.

evidence.note: “It will no more be called Topheth, or the valley of the son of Hinnom, but the valley of slaughter (גֵּיא הַהֲרֵגָה); and they will bury in Topheth for lack of room.”
The same renaming at the potsherd gate.
“Drag them out like sheep for slaughter (לְטִבְחָה), and set them apart for the day of slaughter (הֲרֵגָה).”
“Shepherd the flock of slaughter (צֹאן הַהֲרֵגָה)”, whose buyers kill them (יַהַרְגֻן) and hold themselves guiltless (Zec 11:5).

evidence.locator: Jer.12.3; Zec.11.4, 7, הֲרֵגָה → σφαγῆς; σφαγή renders הֲרֵגָה ×3

evidence.note: The rich “have fattened your hearts in a day of slaughter (ἐν ἡμέρᾳ σφαγῆς)”: the “day of slaughter” of Jer 12:3.
“We were counted as sheep of slaughter (πρόβατα σφαγῆς)”, there for טִבְחָה of Psa 44:23.

parallels.note: “Slaughter” as of sheep: the day of slaughter beside sheep for slaughter.

phrases.gloss: the valley of slaughter (the valley of Hinnom)

cognates.note: Moabite, the Mesha stele: Mesha took Ataroth and Nebo and slew their people, “ואהרג את כל העמ” (line 11) and “ואהרג כלה”, all of it, seven thousand (line 16): the slaughter of a taken city, as Jos 8:24.

evidence.note: Line 11 ואהרג את כל העמ; line 16 ואהרג כלה.
"slew all of it, 7000 men".

cognates.note: Sabaic: the verb of killing in war (“he killed them, three thousand”) and the noun mhrg, the killings of a campaign, as Hebrew הָרַג and הֶרֶג.

evidence.note: v. KILL: R3945/18 hrghmw ṯlṯt ʾlfm “he killed them (to the number of) three thousand”; Gt “beat one another to death”; tp “effect a slaughter”; n. mhrg(m), mhrgtm “slaughters, killings”.

cognates.gloss: slaughter; civil strife and confusion; (of people) fall into strife, confusion and slaughter
cognates.note: Arabic ج answers to Hebrew ג. The Arabic root's common sense is confusion and disorder; slaughter is the sense of the noun in the tradition of the signs of the last day, where Lane notes it is so explained, and that the word is said to be Abyssinian.

evidence.locator: Book I, p. 2890, art. هرج, هَرْجٌ (n41120)
evidence.note: “Trial, or civil war … and confusion, or disorder: vehement and much slaughter … or slaughter; as explained by Mohammad himself.”

evidence.locator: Book I, p. 2890, art. هرج, هَرِجَ (n41116)
evidence.note: هَرَجَ النَّاسُ “The people fell into a state of … civil war or conflict … and confusion, or disorder, and slaughter.”

doctrine.statement: Yahweh renamed the valley of the son of Hinnom, where Judah burned its children (Jer 7:31), “the valley of slaughter”: “they will bury in Topheth for lack of room, and the carcasses of this people will be food for the birds of the heavens” (Jer 7:32–33; 19:6–7). It is a place of the slain, their bodies unburied. Isaiah ends with the same sight: those who come to worship “shall go out and look on the carcasses (פִּגְרֵי) of the men who have transgressed against me; for their worm shall not die, their fire shall not be quenched” (Isa 66:24). Jesus, warning of being “thrown into the valley of Hinnom (γέεννα)”, describes it in Isaiah's words, “where their worm does not die and the fire is not quenched” (Mrk 9:47–48). From the verses: the valley of Hinnom is the valley of slaughter, where the dead bodies of the condemned are consumed; it is the end of the wicked in death and destruction, not the torment of living souls.

In Ezekiel's valley the bones are “very dry” (Ezk 37:2), and the prophet is told to say to the breath, “breathe into these slain (הֲרוּגִים), that they may live”; the breath came into them, “and they lived and stood on their feet” (Ezk 37:9–10). Yahweh explains: “I will open your graves and cause you to come up out of your graves, my people, and bring you into the land of Israel … and I will put my spirit in you, and you shall live, and I will place you in your own land” (Ezk 37:12–14). Isaiah says the same: “your dead shall live … the earth shall cast out the dead”, and “the earth will disclose her blood, and will no more cover her slain” (Isa 26:19, 21). From the verses: the slain are dead until God's breath is put into them again, as it was first breathed into man (Gen 2:7); their life returns in a bodily resurrection from the graves, and it brings them into the land of Israel.

Zechariah is told to shepherd “the flock of slaughter”, whose buyers kill them and are not held guilty, for Yahweh “will no longer pity the inhabitants of the land” but will deliver each “into the hand of his king” (Zec 11:4–6). The shepherd is valued at thirty pieces of silver, which are thrown to the potter in the house of Yahweh, and he breaks his staffs Favour and Union (Zec 11:10–14). Matthew says this was fulfilled when the chief priests bought the potter's field with the price of Jesus (Mat 27:9–10); and the people answered Pilate, “We have no king but Caesar” (Jhn 19:15). Jesus foretold that Jerusalem's enemies would surround her and not leave one stone upon another, “because you did not know the time of your visitation”, and that the people would fall by the edge of the sword (Luk 19:43–44; 21:20–24). From the verses: the flock of slaughter is Israel that rejected its shepherd for thirty pieces of silver, and its slaughter came when the Romans took Jerusalem in AD 70.

note: Takes all three BDB keys: e.cc.aa (verb, 167), e.cc.ab (הֶרֶג, 5), e.cc.ac (הֲרֵגָה, 5). No proper name is formed from the root (none in TIPNR). The brief's one 'qal passive' token, Psa 44:23 הֹרַגְנוּ, is entered under pual with Isa 27:7 הֹרָג, since the stem list has no qal passive; both may be qal passives. The qal passive participle הֲרוּגִים 'the slain' (Ezk 37:9; Isa 26:21; Pro 7:26) is a sense of the qal. The brief found no NT quotation by alignment, but Act 7:28 (Exo 2:14), Rom 11:3 (1Ki 19:10) and Rom 8:36 (Psa 44:23) quote verses using the verb; Mat 23:35 (φονεύω) may recall 2Ch 24:22 and is not cited as a quotation. Cognates: Ugaritic hrg rests on Anderson–Moser and Wiktionary only; Segert's glossary does not list it, so find its texts in DULAT. Aramaic HRG rests on Anderson–Moser only; Jastrow's הָרַג is marked Biblical Hebrew and its uses are Mishnaic Hebrew, so find an Aramaic attestation (CAL; Klein's lead says Old Aramaic). Arabic هرج: is slaughter the root's own sense, or (as Lane's 'in the language of Abyssinia' suggests) a borrowing? Check Ge'ez in Dillmann/Leslau. Mandaic HRG 'rub, grate; be cunning' (Drower–Macuch) does not share the meaning and is left out as likely another root. Contrast with רָצַח (murder) is stated from usage only, not argued from רצח's own entry.
